title: Engineering a city-scale parcel-mapping practice
subtitle: How a core team of about ten delivered 1.5 million+ attributed land parcels across 35–40 cities on five continents, often several cities at once, and the workflow, automation and planning that made it repeatable.

meta.label: Team
meta.value: Core team of ~10; 20+ hired and trained

glance.text: real cities as clean, addressed land parcels for a global platform, all to one delivery standard.
a ten-stage workflow checked at two levels, scripts around the GIS work, and a planning model.

chapters.label: Brief
chapters.heading: Every parcel, every city, one standard
chapters.body:
The cities spanned Europe, the Americas, Australia, the Middle East and East Asia, and several were usually in production at once. The founding partner led the consultancy from the Netherlands while pursuing higher studies there; I led the work on the ground in India: production, systems, hiring, training and the weekly client relationship.

*The client is not named here. The workflow is shown only at the level of its four groups, and the interactive parts use fictional data or real geometry with location, addresses and attributes removed.*
chapters.lead: Real cities as plot-level land parcels: clean polygons with addresses and attributes, ready to load into a global metaverse real-estate platform.

chapters.label: Workflow
chapters.heading: Ten stages in four groups, checked at two levels
chapters.body: Every stage had a written workflow procedure, so a new team member could produce consistent work within days. Every city started with a preparation protocol and market research on local property prices, so the price per square foot used for it stayed close to real market rates.
chapters.lead: Each neighbourhood is checked twice, at the mapping review and the final clean, and each city once more as a whole.

cards.title: Spatial
cards.text: Parcels digitised in QGIS to our mapping criteria, or third-party data reworked to them where the client preferred it. Reviewed, then geometry-cleaned.

cards.title: Textual
cards.text: An address for every parcel, cleaned and standardised to the client's format.

cards.title: Spatial + textual
cards.text: Addresses checked against the map: consistent numbering along each street, no repeats, each landing on its own parcel. Where quality is decided.

cards.title: Quality
cards.text: Each neighbourhood final-cleaned as a finished product; a manager-level review signs off the city.

chapters.label: Automation
chapters.heading: Where scripts took over
chapters.body: Rule-based work moved into scripts that ran alongside the GIS work. Each change below replaced a manual step; people now handled only the exceptions the scripts flagged.

note.title: About 1,500 hours saved on address work
note.body: 1.5 h per 1,000 parcels by hand × ~1,000,000 parcels processed after the automation went live ≈ 1,500 hours. Each automated run takes about 0.25 h whatever its size. An estimate from the measured manual rate, not a logged total.

compare.before: Topology checked and corrected by hand
compare.after: Scripted checks; manual fixes down by about 95% (from around 600 to around 10)

compare.before: Three separate stages: extraction, cleaning, merging · about 1.5 h per 1,000 parcels
compare.after: One automated step: geocoding API, auto-clean, auto-check, fix · a fixed run of about 0.25 h, however many parcels

compare.before: A random sample checked by hand
compare.after: Every address in the batch checked, usually the whole city

compare.before: Output shaped to the client spec by hand
compare.after: Output shaped to the client schema and checked against the delivery criteria automatically

chapters.label: Planning
chapters.heading: A planning model for the manager's view
chapters.body:
To commit to delivery dates with a small team and several cities in parallel, I built a capacity and deadline model, with AI help on the formula logic. It was my management tool, not a product. It takes a city's scope, the team's real availability and everything that eats into it (admin, onboarding, holidays, unplanned leave and unplanned work), and gives a dated plan in two scenarios. The cautious one, with buffers, was the date we committed to.

In use, its finish dates held at about **95% accuracy** against actual completion.

Try it below. The people and the city in it are fictional; change anything and the dates update.

chapters.label: Operations
chapters.heading: Running parallel cities with a small team
chapters.body:
Each **city was a project**, each **stage a list** with its own checklist, and **dashboards with time tracking** showed where every neighbourhood stood and who was on it.

I also owned the people side end to end, and wrote the documentation that held it together: workflow processes, technology, administrative and hiring processes, and user manuals for every automation and tool we built.
chapters.lead: Up to three cities in parallel, run through ClickUp and the planning model.

chapters.label: Client & growth
chapters.heading: Owning the relationship
chapters.body:
Weekly progress and strategy reports, and scope questions handled city by city. I drafted the pre-final **client–consultant service agreement** from scratch, legal terms included.

I was also involved in business development, with market research and stakeholder interviews on where the practice could grow.
chapters.lead: The client's primary contact for more than three years.

chapters.label: Reflection
chapters.heading: What I'd build next
chapters.body:
Everything above is **rule-based**: procedures, scripts and checks written and tuned by hand. It scaled to 35–40 cities, but every new edge case still needed someone to write the next rule, and the plan still ran on fixed benchmarks. What I'd build next:

- **Quality gates as automated tests.** One versioned spatial database for every city, with each QA gate run as a test on every change, the way software is tested before release. Every parcel would carry its history: what changed, who changed it, and which check it passed.
- **Review only where a model is unsure.** In the spatial + textual stage, learn from delivered cities how addresses run along streets, score every parcel, and send people only the low-confidence ones. Their decisions become the next round of training data.
- **Plans that update themselves.** Feed the throughput the pipeline actually records back into the planning model, so finish dates move as the work moves, with a confidence range instead of a single date.

That's the gap I want to close with formal training in spatial data science and GeoAI.
